facts.claim: "Snowbank Blues" is credited to all four band members as writers and composers: Joshua Harmon, Jonas Swanson, Juice Welch and KJ Ward.
David Greenbaum is credited as producer, mixer and engineer on the album, and on "Snowbank Blues" specifically.

On "Snowbank Blues", Harmon is credited with acoustic guitar and vocals, Swanson with electric guitar and background vocals, and Welch with drums. Additional performers credited include Emily Elkin, Heather Lockie and Eric Clark.
According to Harmon, the song began as a way to make his father laugh by imitating the riff of a classic country tune. He then realised the parody had potential.

Harmon said he and Swanson made a garage-band demo in about two hours, using a rice-filled Altoid case as a shaker and improvising the structure. They tried to capture the same DIY feel in the studio recording.
A stop-motion video for "Snowbank Blues", animated and directed by Colin Lepper, premiered at the Utah Museum of Contemporary Art.
It is track 6 on Waiting to Spill and runs about 3:17.
Waiting to Spill was released October 28, 2022 on Capitol Records. It is the band's sophomore album and was produced by six-time Grammy-winning producer David Greenbaum.
The band self-produced their 2019 debut When We Were Friends and had not worked with a producer before Greenbaum.
The Backseat Lovers formed in 2018 in Provo, Utah. Joshua Harmon and Jonas Swanson, who met in a queue for an open-mic night, brought in Juice Welch on drums and, later, KJ Ward on bass.

research.lineage: The song sits in the 2020s Utah indie-rock tradition, with influences the band has cited including Cage the Elephant, Arctic Monkeys, Vampire Weekend and Pinegrove.

draft:
**Snowbank Blues** started as a bit. Joshua Harmon has said he was imitating the riff of a classic country tune to make his father laugh, then realised the parody had real potential. He and Jonas Swanson knocked out a garage demo in about two hours, improvising the structure and shaking a rice-filled Altoid case for percussion. That origin explains a lot. The song opens on the stock phrases of a working-stiff lament: the boss, the daily grind, smoking with friends to get through the night. Then it quietly stops joking.

The turn comes before the first verse is out. Harmon sings, "Catching up on sleep's harder when I'm waking up next to me." It's a clever line, a near-pun on sleeping alone, and it's also the loneliest thing in the song. Someone is gone, a thousand miles off. The narrator is left with a girl down the road sending looks and a question he asks out loud so he doesn't have to answer it: how can he say no when you're that far away? Self-justification and longing arrive in the same breath, and the song doesn't sort them out.

Then the frame widens. Coffee, cameras in his face, too many people in this place, a mask shelved and a stage to take. He admits the smile isn't for himself, that something on his chest is wearing on his health. It's the strain of being watched while missing someone. The refrain pins it to place: he'd roll the windows down if the snow hadn't swallowed the town. Even the urge to get out is snowed in. When he says tomorrow he'll be gone, maybe a thousand miles away, he's measuring himself against the distance she put between them.

The sound keeps the demo's promise. A fingerpicked guitar line, clean and bright, moves at an easy, moderate pace. Harmon's voice is slightly raspy and conversational, with no harmonies around it. Strummed chords fill things out, and when the drums arrive with a plain kick-snare-hi-hat beat, the groove stops ambling and starts to push. The production is dry and close, raw rather than buffed. That's the feel the band said they tried to carry from the garage into the studio, on their first record made with an outside producer, David Greenbaum.

The last lines drop the cool. He grants that she had to leave, and then the accusation comes: "But you didn't have the right / To take the sun." It's unfair, and he half knows it. That's why it stings.

The song leaves you holding that lopsided grief, the kind that understands why someone had to go and still blames them for the cold.
